root.note: Classical Latin fēria meant ‘holiday, feast day’. In Church Latin the days of Easter week, and then of every week, were counted as feriae.

history: Almost every language in Europe names Monday after the Moon and the other days after gods and planets. Portuguese counts. Monday is segunda-feira, the second day, then come terça, quarta, quinta and sexta-feira, Tuesday to Friday. Sunday was the first day. The system comes from Church Latin, which numbered the weekdays as feriae: secunda fēria, tertia fēria, and so on. Old Portuguese still had an older pagan name for Monday, lũes, but the Church numbers won, and Portuguese is the only major Romance language that kept them. In daily speech people simply say segunda or à segunda, ‘on Monday’. A feira today is also a market, like the Feira da Ladra in Lisbon.
historyEinfach: Segunda-feira means ‘Monday’. In Portuguese, the weekdays have numbers: segunda (second), terça (third), quarta (fourth), quinta (fifth), sexta (sixth). Sunday is the first day. The names come from the Latin of the Church. Other languages use the Moon and old gods for the day names.

chain: Latin dies Lunae ‘day of the Moon’
elsewhere.text: Spanish, like most of Europe, named Monday after the Moon.
A fair was a market held on a feast day, the same fēria that counts the Portuguese days.
